doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: The CD The Man From the South and its distribution
summary: He describes his latest CD with Bob Barnard on LaBrava, its title, his 1953 Holden on the cover and the difficulty of distribution.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Tell me about this nice CD.

That’s my latest one, recorded in Australia with master cornet player Bob Barnard. And it’s called “The Man From the South,” which is a tune taken from a Ted Weems recording from 1927. There’s a picture of my car on the front, I’m sitting on my car, which is a 1953 Holden, a brand that will probably be unfamiliar to all the listeners, probably apart from expatriates. MR. Is it a V-8?
No. It’s what they call a small 6, which is as big as you got in those days. Ford had a V-8 but then it cost more. But this was built in Australia and everyone was really proud of it.
And you play trombone, and cornet and you do some vocal, some tenor sax. Well I’ll look forward to hearing this.
Yeah. There’s a clarinet track, I sing a couple, Bob sings one or two.
And you do some arrangements too.
Yep. And it’s out on a label called LaBrava, which is run by the brother of my fiance. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-
You get distribution across Australia — I mean is that the goal? It’s kind of hard sometimes promoting your own records.

Yeah it is. You sell more of them on the gig. David tries his best to contact, he’s got lots and lots of CDs to sell and they’re all really well done, etcetera, etcetera. But he tries to put them in record stores and the mainstream record stores don’t really want to know. All the jazz record stores said fine, but if it’s not the large selling things, they might keep a couple of copies, and when those go they don’t bother reordering because they forget. So distribution is tough, really tough.
